title: A balance, not a gauge
allegory: Logit difference is like weighing the right answer against the wrong one on a balance: whatever lands equally in both pans cancels, every helper's weights simply add to the tilt, and unlike a percentage gauge the beam never pins at the top.
map: weight added equally to both pans changes nothing
anything the two logits share cancels, including the softmax normaliser
each helper drops weights in a pan; the tilt is their total
linear in the residual stream: per-component terms add up (DLA)
a percentage gauge that pins near 100%
probability saturating near 1 and hiding an intervention's effect

chapters.name: The pinned gauge
chapters.note: p(Mary): 97% ... 96%. Did my patch do anything?

cap.1: You change something inside the model and check how likely 'Mary' is: 97%, then 96%. Did your change matter? A gauge stuck near 100% can't tell you.
cap.2: Probability saturates: once the model is confident, big internal changes barely move p(correct). A metric that hides an intervention's effect is useless for finding where a behaviour lives.
cap.3: softmax compresses large logit changes near p ≈ 1, so probability is a poor, nonlinear readout of interventions. You want a signed metric that moves both ways and is linear in the residual stream.

props.label: same weight in both pans: no tilt

cap.1: Instead, weigh 'Mary' against 'John' on a balance. Weight added to both pans changes nothing; only the difference tips the beam, either way.
cap.2: Logit difference = logit(Mary) − logit(John). Anything that pushes both names up equally, like a general 'a name comes next' signal, cancels. What's left is the model's preference between the two.
cap.3: logit[IO] − logit[S] = log(p(IO)/p(S)): the softmax normaliser cancels, as does any shared component. It's the log-odds between the two candidates, unbounded in both directions.

cap.1: The tilt has a plain meaning: how many times likelier Mary is than John, on a log scale. Zero means a tie. Every +1 multiplies Mary's odds by about 2.7.
cap.2: The softmax divides both probabilities by the same total, so that total cancels in the ratio. The logit difference is exactly the log of p(Mary)/p(John), and it never saturates.
cap.3: Δ = (W_U[:, IO] − W_U[:, S]) · ln_final(x): one fixed direction dotted with the final residual. That linearity is why DLA can split Δ exactly into per-component terms.

curves.label: Mary's share of the two names, sigmoid(Δ)

cap.1: Here's why the gauge gets stuck. As the tilt grows, the probability flattens out near 100%. Doubling the tilt from 3 to 6 moves it from 95% to 99.8%.
cap.2: With two candidates, p(Mary) = sigmoid(Δ). The curve is flat at both ends, so a large internal change can look tiny in probability, while Δ moves one-for-one with what the model wrote.
cap.3: dp/dΔ = p(1 − p) → 0 as p → 1: probability metrics lose sensitivity exactly where a well-performing model sits. Δ has unit slope and stays linear in each component's write.

chapters.name: Every helper's share
chapters.title: the tilt splits into one term per component

cap.1: Every part of the model just drops weights into the pans, so you can ask each part what it added. A few push hard for Mary; a few push for John.
cap.2: Direct logit attribution: dot each head's output with the Mary-minus-John direction. On IOI, heads 9.6 and 9.9 push toward the right name; 10.7 and 11.10 push against it.
cap.3: A linear metric of an additive stream: per-component terms sum exactly to Δ once the final LayerNorm scale is applied (apply_ln_to_stack). Assert the sum matches the model's actual Δ.

chapters.name: Cancel, then rescale

left.title: Raw, one prompt
lines: John favoured by about 1 logit anyway

chapters.verdict: Cancel what you don't care about, then scale so 0 and 1 mean something.

cap.1: Two more tricks: swap which name is the answer across examples so built-in favouritism cancels, then rescale so 0 means broken and 1 means fixed.
cap.2: GPT-2's final layernorm bias alone favours 'John' over 'Mary' by about a logit, so IOI uses matched prompt pairs. For patching, report (patched − corrupted) / (clean − corrupted).
cap.3: Average Δ over ABBA/ABAB pairs so name-frequency priors and fixed biases cancel. Normalise so corrupted reads 0 and clean reads 1, and say whether it's denoising or noising, since the sign flips.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: One number that moves both ways
The yardstick for patching and steering

cap.1: A good yardstick is half of interpretability. This one moves both ways, never gets stuck, and splits into each part's share: who did what.
cap.2: Logit difference is the metric behind DLA, activation patching and path patching in [1.4.1]. When you steer a model later, the same contrast tells you whether you moved the behaviour you meant.
cap.3: A task-specific contrast, unlike cross-entropy's general objective: signed, linear in the residual stream, cancelling shared structure. Choosing it is the first design decision of any causal analysis.

curves.f: exp(x + s)/(exp(x + s) + exp(b + s) + exp(2))
curves.label: p(Mary) as Mary's logit varies (rest of vocab = 2)
Mary's share of the two names, sigmoid(Δ)

caption.1: Slide the shared push: both names rise, p(Mary) wobbles, the logit difference doesn't budge. Push Mary past 5 and p(Mary) stops responding.
caption.2: p(Mary) depends on everything (John, the rest of the vocabulary, shared pushes) and saturates. Δ = logit(Mary) − logit(John) depends only on the contrast, and p(Mary)/p(John) = e^Δ exactly.
caption.3: Adding s to both logits leaves Δ invariant but moves mass to or from the 'other' bucket, changing p(Mary). Δ is shift-invariant, unbounded and linear in the residual stream; probability is none of these.

where_else: Reward models in RLHF score preferences as sigmoid(r_A − r_B): a difference of scores
Log-odds in statistics and logistic regression: a probability ratio on a log scale
Steering and probing metrics: measure a behaviour as 'desired token minus undesired token'

hamming.what: The model's score for the right answer minus its score for the tempting wrong one: the log of how many times likelier one is than the other.
hamming.when: Whenever you intervene inside a model (attribution, patching, steering) and need to measure the effect on one specific choice.
hamming.why: It cancels everything the two answers share, never saturates, and is linear in the residual stream, so effects add up and can be split per component.

object.title: The balance sheet
object.subtitle: One sheet, two readings: a probability that plateaus, or a logit difference that ramps forever.

cap.1: Height is how likely 'Mary' is as Mary's and John's scores change. Notice the big flat plateau: once Mary is ahead, the height barely moves.
cap.2: The probability surface p(Mary) over (logit Mary, logit John), with the rest of the vocabulary lumped into one 'other' logit.
cap.3: softmax over {Mary, John, other}: a sigmoid-like sheet that saturates at 1, where its gradient vanishes.

cap.1: Raise the 'everything else' score: the whole sheet sags, although nothing changed between Mary and John.
cap.2: p(Mary) depends on the rest of the vocabulary too, so it mixes in things your experiment never touched.
cap.3: Probability is not invariant to other logits: the softmax normaliser couples every token.

cap.1: Switch to the balance reading: the sheet becomes a flat ramp. Every step toward Mary tilts it by the same amount, forever.
cap.2: Logit difference Δ = logit(Mary) − logit(John): a plane, linear, never saturating, zero along the tie line.
cap.3: Δ is linear in (logit M, logit J), hence linear in the residual stream through W_U: the property DLA and patching rely on.

cap.1: Move 'everything else' again: the ramp doesn't move at all. The balance ignores whatever lands in both pans or outside them.
cap.2: Δ is untouched by the other logits and by any push shared by both names.
cap.3: Invariant to the normaliser and to common-mode shifts: only the contrast direction W_U[:, IO] − W_U[:, S] matters.

cap.1: From above, the tie line runs corner to corner. On one side Mary wins, on the other John does, and the height says by how much.
cap.2: Contours of Δ are parallel lines; each unit step multiplies the odds of Mary over John by e.
cap.3: Level sets of Δ are exactly the level sets of p(M)/p(J) = e^Δ.

predict.q: A patch moves p(Mary) from 0.97 to 0.96. What can you conclude?

options.t: Not much: probability is saturated here, so check the logit difference
The patch had almost no effect

predict.why: Near 1 the probability curve is flat, so a large internal change can look tiny.

predict.q: A head raises logit(Mary) and logit(John) by the same amount. Its effect on the logit difference?

options.t: It depends on the rest of the vocabulary

predict.why: Equal weight in both pans cancels. Δ only measures the contrast.

predict.q: The logit difference is 2. How many times likelier is Mary than John?
predict.why: Δ = log(p(Mary)/p(John)), so the ratio is e² ≈ 7.39.

object.where: Anywhere two options are compared: log-odds in statistics, preference scores in reward models, contrastive probes.
